amsterdam-nl.intro:
Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, and its financial, cultural and creative heart, with more than 900,000 residents. It is known for its canals, impressive architecture, museums and art galleries, and more than 1,500 bridges, and it has earned the title "Venice of the North". A humble fishing village in the late 12th century, it became a bustling trading hub in the 17th century.

Most visitors experience the city centre, a semi-circle with Centraal Station at its apex and a radius of about 2 km. Five concentric canals ring it (Singel, Herengracht, Keizersgracht, Prinsengracht and Singelgracht) and form the Canal District; the Canal Belt gained UNESCO World Heritage status in 2010. The Jordaan and Plantage are other districts inside the centre.

The centre is compact and pretty flat, so most tourist destinations are within walking distance, and most areas are within half an hour of Centraal Station. The city is very bike-friendly, with separate bike lanes on most major streets, and cycling is the main mode of transport for most locals. English is widely spoken and understood by almost everyone.

barcelona-es.intro:
Barcelona is Spain's second-largest city and the capital of Catalonia, a major port on the north-eastern Mediterranean coast. It was founded more than 2,000 years ago as the Roman town Barcino. Its many faces include the medieval Old Town, the distinctive street grid from 19th-century urban planning, long sandy beaches and green parks on the hills, and prominent buildings by the architect Antoni Gaudí, including the Sagrada Família.

Barcelona El Prat is the main airport, with a metro station at both terminals. The metro is an efficient way to get around, and public transport across the area shares an integrated fare system. Catalan and Spanish are the official languages, and in tourist areas almost all shops and bars have some English-speaking staff.

August is probably the busiest month, but many shops and restaurants close from early August to early September while residents are away. The most comfortable weather, 19–23 °C, is usually from May to June and from late August to October.

berlin-de.intro:
Berlin is Germany's capital and largest city, with 3.7 million residents within the city limits (2022). "Arm aber sexy" (poor but sexy), as a former mayor put it, Berlin attracts young people, students and a creative bohème. Its architecture reflects Prussian monarchism, Nazism and East German communism, plus the 1990s and 2000s glass palaces of Potsdamer Platz, and it is as varied as its neighbourhoods and its people. Berlin is home to world-renowned universities, orchestras, museums and entertainment venues, and its Zoological Garden is the most visited zoo in Europe.

Berlin can be seen as a cluster of centres. Mitte might be thought of as the core, but it is often not where locals' lives revolve. The city has 12 boroughs (Bezirke), each made up of several localities (Kiez or Viertel) with a unique style, and almost all of them have what you need for daily life a short walk from your lodging, with easy access to a metro station.

Public transport (U-Bahn, S-Bahn, bus, tram and regional rail) shares one zone-based ticket system, with zones A, B and C. If you need to get around the city quickly, take the S-Bahn.

florence-it.intro:
Florence (Italian: Firenze) is the capital of the region of Tuscany in Italy, and its historic centre is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list. It is a cultural, artistic and architectural gem and the birthplace of the Italian Renaissance, home in its day to powerful families, creative geniuses and scientific masterminds who left their legacies in the city's museums and art galleries. It is also the birthplace of the poet Dante, and standard Italian is primarily based on the Tuscan dialect spoken here.

Most major sights are within easy walking distance of each other; you can walk from one end of the historic centre to the other in half an hour. The city runs a bike rental service, and almost all of the historic centre is flat, although traffic can be terrible.

Almost all trains stop at Firenze Santa Maria Novella on the north edge of the old town, near most accommodation and sights. Amerigo Vespucci airport, locally known as Peretola, is 4 km north-west of the centre and is connected to the station by tram line T2.
florence-it.review_note: Reviewed against Wikivoyage 'Florence' revision 5350936 and rewritten from the generated draft; every kept statement is supported by that page. Corrected: Draft said taxis are 'readily available'; the page says a taxi is hard to hail and best called ahead by your hotel or restaurant. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

funchal-pt.intro:
Funchal is the capital and main city of the autonomous region of Madeira, on the south of the island of Madeira. Its name comes from funcho, the Portuguese word for the fennel that grows abundantly there, and it was an important shipping centre in the 15th to 17th centuries.

The city centre is small enough to explore on foot, and orange city buses run around town and up to Monte. Sights include the Mercado dos Lavradores (Peasants' Market), the Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro park and the Madeira Botanical Garden. The Funchal Cable Car climbs to Monte, and at Monte you can ride a wooden toboggan down the mountain on a 2 km roadway, steered by men.

Cristiano Ronaldo Madeira International Airport is about 30 minutes north-east of the city, in Santa Cruz municipality. By road, the city is served by the coastal highway ER101. Motorcycles and mopeds are a common way to explore the island.
funchal-pt.review_note: Reviewed against Wikivoyage 'Funchal' revision 5367473 and rewritten from the generated draft; every kept statement is supported by that page. Corrected: Draft called the toboggan ride an 'activity' without saying where; the page places it at Monte and describes men steering the sledge. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

istanbul-tr.intro:
Istanbul is the most populous city in Europe, with more than 14 million people, and the financial and cultural centre of Turkey. It straddles the border between Asia and Europe on either side of the Bosphorus. The Bosphorus Strait, the Golden Horn estuary and the Sea of Marmara divide the city, and the Black Sea forms its relatively less developed northern boundary.

Most sights are concentrated in the old city on the Sultanahmet peninsula, on the European side between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara. Across the Horn to the north are Galata, Beyoğlu and Taksim, the heart of modern Istanbul, while Kadıköy is the major district on the comparatively less-visited Anatolian side.

Istanbul has two main airports, Istanbul Airport on the European side and Sabiha Gökçen International Airport on the Asian side. Within the city, the İstanbulkart smart card works on buses, trams, suburban trains, the metro and local ferries, and ferries cross the Bosphorus.

Despite stereotypes of a sunny, warm holiday destination, Istanbul has an oceanic climate with some Mediterranean influences: very warm, mostly sunny summers, and cool to chilly, bleak winters with very frequent rain and, on occasion, snow.
istanbul-tr.review_note: Reviewed against Wikivoyage 'Istanbul' revision 5363386 and rewritten from the generated draft; every kept statement is supported by that page. kyoto-jp.intro:
Kyoto was the capital of Japan and the residence of the Emperor from 794 until the Meiji Restoration of 1868, and it carries a reputation as the nation's most beautiful city and its cultural capital. First impressions are of the urban sprawl around the ultra-modern glass-and-steel train station, but the temples and parks that ring the city centre reward a longer look. Kyoto was among the few Japanese cities that escaped the bombings of World War II, so it still has many prewar buildings, including traditional townhouses known as machiya.

The city core still follows the grid adopted in 794. West-east streets are numbered, from Ichijō-dōri (First Street) in the north to Jūjō-dōri (Tenth Street) in the south, while there is no obvious pattern to the names of north-south streets.

Kyoto has no airport of its own. It is served by Osaka's two airports, Kansai International and Itami, with an excellent road and railway network between the two cities, and most visitors arrive at JR Kyoto Station by Shinkansen from Tokyo. Kyoto has four seasons: flowers in spring and changing leaves in autumn attract crowds, summer is humid, the rainy season runs from about mid-June to the end of July, and winters are generally cold but without snowfall.

lisbon-pt.intro:
Lisbon (Portuguese: Lisboa) is the capital of Portugal, built on seven hills at the wide mouth of the Tagus (Tejo), where the river meets the Atlantic Ocean. It is known for its white limestone buildings, intimate alleyways and an easy-going charm.

The slopes are one of Lisbon's trademarks, so getting around can be a workout. The elegant squares and broad avenues of the lower town give way to the narrow, winding streets of districts such as Alfama and Bairro Alto, and old trams run alongside an efficient metro network. Most points of interest lie in a compact area around Praça do Comércio on the river, where the pedestrianised grid of Baixa begins; Baixa borders the historic quarters of Alfama, Chiado and Bairro Alto.

Greater Lisbon includes Sintra, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the seaside resorts of Estoril and Cascais. The climate is Subtropical-Mediterranean, with mild winters and very warm summers. The ocean makes the weather windy and fast-changing, so bring a jacket or umbrella in winter, spring and autumn.

london-gb.intro:
London, the capital and largest city of the United Kingdom, sits on the River Thames in South-East England. Greater London has a little over 9 million people. London is considered one of the world's leading global cities and an international capital of culture, music, education, fashion, politics, finance and trade, with a seemingly endless choice of historical sites, shopping, museums, food, art galleries and nightlife.

The name "London" once referred only to the walled "Square Mile", now called the City of London, and the city has since absorbed many surrounding towns and villages. Greater London consists of 32 London Boroughs and the City of London.

The Tube, the world's oldest rapid transit system, has 11 lines covering the central area and northern suburbs, while National Rail services mainly cover the southern suburbs. All London airports have direct public transport connections to the centre. In central London, walking to the next Tube station often takes about 10 minutes.

marrakesh-ma.intro:
Marrakech (also spelt Marrakesh) is one of the imperial cities of Morocco and its main tourist destination. It is the fourth largest city in Morocco and lies near the foothills of the snow-capped Atlas Mountains, a few hours from the foot of the Sahara Desert.

The city has two parts. The Medina, the historical city, is full of intertwining narrow passageways and local shops, and it holds the large square Djemaa El-Fna, where many hotels are located and where tourists, locals and vendors congregate. Gueliz, also called Ville Nouvelle, is the modern district, with modern restaurants, fast food chains and big-brand stores.

Scams aimed at tourists are widespread; even locals call the city "Marrakech, Arnakech" ("Marrakech, Scam"). Marrakech-Menara Airport, about 9 km south-west of the Medina, has flights from many European cities, including low-cost carriers. The L19 airport shuttle bus runs to Djemaa El-Fna, and a petit taxi ride into the centre takes 10 to 15 minutes. For a romantic alternative in town, hire a caleche, a small horse-drawn carriage.

mexico-city-mx.intro:
Mexico City (Spanish: Ciudad de México, or CDMX) is the capital of Mexico, its most populous city, and one of the most important financial and cultural centres of the American continent. The city centre is built on the ruins of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan. About 9.2 million people live in the city proper and 22 million in the urban area (2020). It sits in the Valley of Mexico, surrounded on three sides by tall mountains and volcanoes, at an altitude of more than 2,200 m, and its colonial-era Centro Histórico is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The city is divided into 16 alcaldías (boroughs), which are subdivided into around 2,150 colonias (neighborhoods). Visitors do better to think in terms of districts grouped by shared history and clusters of attractions, but knowing which colonia you are going to is essential for getting around.

The city government operates the Metro and the Metrobús bus rapid transit system, which are cheap and reliable but can be very crowded during rush hour. Catching cabs in the street may be dangerous; radio taxis, which you call by phone, are recommended, especially at night. Spanish is the official language, and at most hotels and tour services the personnel also speak English.

new-york-us.intro:
New York, known as "The Big Apple" and "NYC" and often called New York City, is a global centre for media, entertainment, art, fashion, research, finance and trade, and by far the most populous city in the United States. It lies at the mouth of the Hudson River and is home to more than 8 million people. Immigrants and their descendants from over 180 countries live here.

The city consists of five boroughs, each of which is also a county: Manhattan, Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Staten Island. Each borough has a unique culture, and neighborhoods, some only a few blocks in size, have personalities lauded in music and film. "The city" can mean either New York City as a whole or Manhattan alone; the other boroughs are sometimes called the "outer boroughs".

In Manhattan, avenues run north-south and street numbers rise as you move uptown; use "uptown" and "downtown" rather than compass directions. New York generally has all four seasons, with hot and humid summers (Jun-Sept) and mild to very cold winters (Dec-Mar).

paris-fr.intro:
Paris, the cosmopolitan capital of France, has the reputation of being the most beautiful and romantic of all cities, and remains vastly influential in culture, art, fashion, food and design. It sits on the River Seine in north-central France, and about 2 million people live in the city proper, inside the Boulevard Périphérique. A large part of the city, including the banks of the Seine, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its landmarks include the Eiffel Tower, the Arc de Triomphe, Notre-Dame de Paris, the Louvre, the Moulin Rouge and the Basilique du Sacré-Cœur.

The city is divided into 20 arrondissements, numbered from 1 to 20 in a clockwise spiral from the centre. The 12th and 16th arrondissements contain the large parks Bois de Vincennes and Bois de Boulogne. Tourist information centres and hotels provide free city and Métro maps.

Make realistic plans: there are so many attractions that visiting only the famous ones is time-consuming, and they are crowded during major holidays. Leave time for a calm stroll along the back streets, and save some attractions for your next visit.

porto-pt.intro:
Porto is Portugal's second-largest city and the capital of the Northern region, a busy industrial and commercial centre. It is built on high ground overlooking the north side of the Douro estuary. Its historical centre was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, and the site has been inhabited since at least the 4th century BC.

The city is architecturally varied, with medieval and modern buildings side by side, and the ground is very uneven: hard on the feet, but pleasant to the eye. Across the Douro at Vila Nova de Gaia are the warehouses of well-known Port wine companies.

The Porto Metro, a modern light rail and subway system, crosses the centre and reaches surrounding municipalities. It is probably the most efficient way to get around, although some major areas of the city are not well served by it.
porto-pt.review_note: Reviewed against Wikivoyage 'Porto' revision 5355253 and rewritten from the generated draft; every kept statement is supported by that page. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

prague-cz.intro:
Prague (Czech: Praha) is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic and the historic capital of Bohemia. It lies on the banks of the meandering Vltava River, with a castle from the 9th century dominating the skyline. Almost undamaged by World War II, its compact medieval centre is a mixture of cobbled lanes, walled courtyards, cathedrals and church spires.

Wikivoyage divides Prague into ten numbered districts, Praha 1 to Praha 10, a simplified version of the "old" system that appears on street signs and house numbers. Praha 1 is the oldest part of the city and has by far the largest number of attractions; Praha 2 also contains important historic areas. Buildings carry two numbers: a blue orientation number for the position on the street and a red number from the district's house register.

Public transport includes three metro lines and over twenty tram lines. Buses do not enter the historic districts, and Prague is a very walkable city, although almost all of its streets are cobbled. The main tourist information office is in the Old Town Hall at Staroměstské náměstí 1.

rome-it.intro:
Rome, the 'Eternal City', is the capital and largest city of Italy and of the Lazio region, on the River Tiber between the Apennine Mountains and the Tyrrhenian Sea. It was the centre of the Roman Empire, is today the seat of the Italian government, and has about 2.7 million inhabitants. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with palaces, thousand-year-old churches and basilicas, ruins, monuments and fountains.

The historic centre (centro storico) is quite small and lies mainly inside the Aurelian walls. Grand palaces, avenues and basilicas are surrounded by tiny alleyways, little churches and old houses, and modern buildings are mostly in the suburbs. Once you are in the centre, you are best off on foot; buses, trams and the metro are also available.

For two weeks in August many Romans go on holiday and many shops and restaurants close, so expect "Chiuso per ferie" (closed for holidays) signs.
rome-it.review_note: Reviewed against Wikivoyage 'Rome' revision 5355689 and rewritten from the generated draft; every kept statement is supported by that page. Corrected: Draft called the public transport 'efficient'; the page does not, and it warns that the metro gets crowded. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

seville-es.intro:
Seville (Spanish: Sevilla) is the capital of Andalusia. Its heritage comes from the Arabs and from the Age of Discovery, and it also has a flamenco scene, festivals, colour and a thriving nightlife. Tourist facilities are top-notch. The smooth, slow Guadalquivir River flows through the city, which has been a busy port since Roman times, and the city hosted the International Exposition in 1992.

Walking is the best option for sightseeing: Seville is a large city, but the points of interest are in the compact old centre, where fine old churches, charming cafes and hidden plazas are part of the experience.

Buses run frequently and cover the majority of the city, and a rechargeable green travel card gives a lower price on the metro, tram, Cercanías regional trains and buses. The tram is barely 2 km of track through an area you will probably prefer to walk. Sevici bikes can be rented from stations all over town.

Corrected: Wikivoyage ranks Seville Spain's fourth-largest city; Wikipedia now says fifth, so no ranking is shown. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

tavira-pt.intro:
Tavira is a small city in the Algarve region of Portugal, crossed by the Gilão River and known for its monuments, including 37 churches. Its sights include the Castelo de Tavira, of Muslim origin and rebuilt after the Reconquista, whose walls give the best views of the city, and the Igreja da Misericórdia, considered the best example of Renaissance architecture in the Algarve. The Roman Bridge, the best-known bridge in Tavira, dates from around the 16th or 17th century.

The fishing settlements of Cabanas de Tavira and Santa Luzia lie a few kilometres away. Tavira and these settlements give access to the beaches of the Ria Formosa National Park islands, Ilha de Tavira and Ilha de Cabanas.

Tavira is small and perfectly walkable, and a small tour train and electric tuk-tuks are also available. The climate is mild, with hot summers and humid winters. Try the Folhado de Tavira, a puff cake wrapped in sugar. The nearest airport is Faro, a 45-minute drive away.
tavira-pt.review_note: Reviewed against Wikivoyage 'Tavira' revision 5357108 and rewritten from the generated draft; every kept statement is supported by that page. Draft called the castle 'a medieval castle'; the page says it is of Muslim origin and was rebuilt after the Reconquista, with only sections of the wall left. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

tokyo-jp.intro:
Tokyo is the enormous and wealthy capital of Japan, overflowing with culture, commerce and people. Strictly, the capital is Tokyo Metropolis, which is equal in status to a prefecture; this guide covers the 23 special wards, which is what most people mean by "Tokyo". Yokohama, Kawasaki and Chiba blend in seamlessly around them.

The JR Yamanote Line, a loop around central Tokyo, defines its geography: the centre lies within the loop, and the Edo-era old town (shitamachi) is to the north and east. Districts vary wildly, from the electronic blare of Akihabara to the Imperial gardens and shrines of Chiyoda, the youth culture of Shibuya and the pottery shops and temple markets of Asakusa. The subway, the oldest in Asia (opened in 1927), is mainly useful within the Yamanote loop.

You can get around Tokyo without speaking Japanese, since station signs include station names in romaji. Tokyo has a humid subtropical climate; cherry blossoms arrive in March and April, and summers are very humid.

Corrected: Draft said costs 'make it an accessible destination for travelers'; the page only says costs are comparable to other large developed-world cities, so the inference was dropped. Details: tasks/guides-review.md.

vienna-at.intro:
Vienna (German: Wien) is the capital of Austria and by far its most populous city, with an urban population of about 2 million (2.9 million in the metropolitan area, 2023). It is the country's artistic, cultural, economic and political centre, known for its high living standards, relaxed yet elegant lifestyle and rich musical life. It was the seat of the Habsburg court, and Beethoven, Haydn, Liszt, Mozart, Schubert and Johann Strauss II are among the artists it has nurtured. The large historic city centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Vienna is divided into 23 districts, each with a name and a number: the inner districts are 1 to 9 and the outer districts 10 to 23. They vary immensely in size and each has its own flair. The layout is very centralised, radiating from the historic first district, with Stephansdom and Stephansplatz at the centre; the Ringstraße, a grand boulevard, encircles that first district.

Vienna is famous for its coffee-house culture and its electronic music scene, and the Viennese have a singular fascination with death, hence the popularity of the Zentralfriedhof (Central Cemetery) as a strolling location. Public transport includes rail, commuter rail, underground, trams and buses. The underground is very efficient and takes you within a few minutes' walk of almost anywhere you are likely to want to visit.
